performers: The Griller String Quartet: Sidney Griller and Jack O’Brien, violins; Philip Burton, viola; Colin Hampton, cello
intro: Beethoven wrote this movement, a “holy song of thanksgiving” for four string players, after a serious illness in 1825. The Griller Quartet plays the long hymn and the two D major passages, over which Beethoven wrote that he felt new strength.

sections.label: A · Hymn in F Lydian on white notes
sections.mNote: F Lydian; short imitations lead into long held chords.

sections.label: A′ · Return of the hymn with moving accompaniment
sections.mNote: Long violin notes above more active lower strings.

sections.label: B′ · D major dance theme returns
sections.mNote: The violin decorates the tune with quicker notes.

sections.label: A″ · Final hymn, “With the deepest feeling”
sections.mNote: The phrases of the final hymn pass through all four parts.

cues.title: Opening phrase and chorale
cues.text: A short phrase passes from the first violin down through the quartet. The players then move into long chords in hymn style. Beethoven headed the movement “holy song of thanksgiving of a convalescent to the Deity, in the Lydian mode”.
cues.evidence: Beethoven’s heading in Op. 132, III, 1825; our translation. Breitkopf & Härtel, Werke, Serie 6 No. 51, 1863, printed p. 173. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Opus132.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: B natural in the Lydian hymn
cues.text: The hymn centres on F, but its scale has B♮ where F major has B♭. Beethoven’s Lydian mode uses the seven white notes of a keyboard, with F as the final.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 173: Beethoven’s Lydian heading, no key signature, F-centred harmony and B♮.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Illness and completion, 1825
cues.text: In the spring of 1825 a serious illness interrupted Beethoven’s work on this quartet. He returned to it during his recovery and completed it in July. Above the slow movement he wrote his own words of thanksgiving.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus, Beethoven’s String Quartets exhibition guide, pp. 7–8: illness in spring 1825 and completion in July. https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf

cues.title: First Andante, D major
cues.text: The music moves to D major and a faster 3/8. A trill in the first violin is followed by short runs, and the cello carries the tune in brief rising figures. Beethoven marked the section Neue Kraft fühlend (feeling new strength).
cues.evidence: Beethoven’s inscription at the first Andante, Op. 132, III, 1825; our translation. Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 173–174: D major, 3/8, violin trill and rising cello figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the hymn, varied
cues.text: The slow hymn returns, with longer notes in the first violin and moving lines in the lower parts. The other instruments play around the melody, sometimes alternating with it, sometimes continuing while it holds a note. The music is again in F, on the scale of the white notes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 175, Molto adagio: cancelled key signature, common time, sustained first violin and altered lower parts.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Galitzin’s commission, 1822
cues.text: In November 1822 Prince Nikolai Galitzin, an amateur cellist in St Petersburg, asked Beethoven for “one, two or three” quartets, and Beethoven named a fee of 50 ducats each. Galitzin went bankrupt in 1826. His son settled the debt with Beethoven’s nephew Karl in 1835 and 1852.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus Bonn, exhibition guide “The string quartets of Beethoven”, showcase 6 (text by Nicole Kämpken): Galitzin’s request of November 1822, the fee of 50 ducats, the bankruptcy and the payments of 1835 and 1852. https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf

cues.title: Copying the parts, August 1825
cues.text: The parts had to be copied before the quartet could be played. The cellist Joseph Linke worked from the manuscript, but the effort gave him a headache, and the violinist Karl Holz took over the last movement. Beethoven checked and corrected the parts himself.
cues.evidence: Holz’s entry in Beethoven’s conversation book, about 13 August 1825, BKh 8 p. 39, transcribed at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/; Beethoven-Haus guide, pp. 7–8, describes copying and corrections.

cues.title: Letter from Galitzin, 14 January 1826
cues.text: On 14 January 1826 Galitzin wrote that he had read in a Leipzig journal that the new A minor quartet had been played in Vienna. He was so impatient, he said, that he begged Beethoven to send it by post “without further delay”.
cues.evidence: Galitzin to Beethoven, 14 January 1826 (“sans plus tarder par la poste”; our translation): https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/

cues.title: Second Andante in D major
cues.text: D major and the Andante return. The first violin decorates the tune with runs and trills, and the lower strings keep its springing accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 175–177, second Andante: D major, 3/8, ornamented violin line and accompanying figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Paris and Berlin editions, 1827
cues.text: Schlesinger bought this quartet and the F major, Op. 135, for his Paris “Collection complète”. They are the only Beethoven quartets first published outside the German-speaking lands. Schlesinger’s father issued a parallel Berlin edition.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus Bonn, exhibition guide “The string quartets of Beethoven”, showcase 2 on Schlesinger’s “Collection complète” (text by Emil Platen): https://internet.beethoven.de/pdf-sonderausstellung/Beethovens-Streichquartette-Brief-Guide.pdf. Op. 132 published by Schlesinger in Paris and Berlin in 1827: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/

cues.title: Final Molto adagio
cues.text: The marking Mit innigster Empfindung (with the deepest feeling) stands beside each player’s returning phrase. In the final hymn the voices enter one after another, and its long notes and turning figures pass among all four instruments. The dance-like music does not return.
cues.evidence: Beethoven’s instructions at the final Molto adagio, Op. 132, III, 1825; our translation. Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 178–179: successive inscribed entries and final slow span.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rehearsal and first performance, 1825
cues.text: On 8 September 1825 Karl Holz wrote to Beethoven: “Yesterday was the rehearsal of the new quartet; Carl was there too: we were delighted.” George Smart noted that Beethoven himself conducted the players at the first performance the next day.
cues.evidence: Holz in Beethoven’s conversation book, 8 September 1825 (BKh 8, p. 108; our translation); Smart’s notes on the performance of 9 September, reproduced in Thayer–Deiters–Riemann V, pp. 242–244: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/

cues.title: Karl’s report, 6 November 1825
cues.text: After the concert of 6 November 1825, Beethoven’s nephew Karl reported that the hall was “infinitely full”, and that “it went very well together, and Linke played better than ever”.
cues.evidence: Karl van Beethoven in Beethoven’s conversation book (BKh 8, p. 182; our translation): https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/

cues.title: Leipzig review, 1825
cues.text: Reviewing that concert, Leipzig’s Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung said that what “our musical Jean Paul” gave here was “great, splendid, unusual, surprising and original”, and must be studied as well as often heard. The reviewer found a monotony in the very long Adagio.
cues.evidence: Allgemeine musikalische Zeitung, Leipzig, 1825, review of the concert of 6 November (our translation of “gross, herrlich, ungewöhnlich, überraschend und originell … Einförmigkeit in dem sehr langen Adagio”), quoted at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/

cues.title: Vienna review, 24 November 1825
cues.text: A Vienna paper of 24 November 1825 wrote that Beethoven “hurries far ahead of his time” while the understanding of his listeners and critics “still pants laboriously behind”. Its reviewer counted himself among those left behind.
cues.evidence: Wiener Allgemeine Theaterzeitung, No. 18, 24 November 1825, p. 579 (our translation), quoted at https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/

cues.title: Private hearings, September 1825
cues.text: On 9 September 1825 fourteen invited guests heard the quartet at Vienna’s Zum Wilden Mann inn. It was played again two days later, and the visiting British musician George Smart was among the listeners.
cues.evidence: Private hearings of 9 and 11 September 1825, location, guest count and Smart’s attendance: https://www.lvbeethoven.org/opus132/.

cues.title: Final F chord
cues.text: The hymn approaches its final F chord. Moving phrases end in held notes, and Beethoven marks pianissimo. The first violin holds a high note above the cello’s F, and all four players sustain the ending under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 179, end of III: F-major chord, pp and fermatas. The cue retains the established closing passage time.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From F to D major
transitions.from: A · Hymn in F Lydian on white notes
transitions.how: The hymn closes on F, with the first violin holding its upper note under a fermata. Neue Kraft fühlend introduces a D major Andante in 3/8. F♯ and C♯ enter the signature; the first violin trills and the cello starts a short rising figure.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel, Werke, Serie 6 No. 51, printed p. 173. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Opus132.pdf

transitions.title: Return from Andante to the hymn
transitions.to: A′ · Return of the hymn with moving accompaniment
transitions.how: Above a descending cello line the Andante’s violin figures become quieter. At Molto adagio Beethoven cancels the two-sharp signature and restores common time. The F-Lydian hymn returns in long notes in the first violin, and the lower strings move more freely beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 175, first system and following hymn. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Opus132.pdf

transitions.title: Return of the Andante, with ornamentation
transitions.from: A′ · Return of the hymn with moving accompaniment
transitions.to: B′ · D major dance theme returns
transitions.how: The second hymn closes over F in the cello. The bass moves to D, and the two-sharp signature and 3/8 return with Andante. The first violin leaps into the upper register and plays its tune with quicker flourishes above a rising accompaniment in the lower strings.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed pp. 175–176, second Andante. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Opus132.pdf

transitions.title: Andante to the final Molto adagio
transitions.from: B′ · D major dance theme returns
transitions.to: A″ · Final hymn, “With the deepest feeling”
transitions.how: The second Andante ends, and Molto adagio restores common time and F Lydian. Second violin, viola and cello enter in turn, and then the first violin joins their moving phrases. Beethoven wrote Mit innigster Empfindung beside each entry. The hymn’s long notes appear among those lines bit by bit.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score, printed p. 178, final Molto adagio and its inscribed entries. https://www.lvbeethoven.it/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Opus132.pdf

source.title: Beethoven, Op.132 — Breitkopf & Härtel, Beethovens Werke, 1863, plate B.51
source.locator: Printed pp. 173–179, movement III. Two violins, viola and cello, with one player on each part.

timeline.note: The players enter one by one, then play long hymn chords.
The first violin trills and runs above short rising figures in the lower strings.
Long first-violin notes carry the hymn above moving phrases in the other three parts.
The returning D-major tune gains quicker flourishes in the first violin.
Each player takes up the phrases of the final hymn; long violin notes sound above them towards the quiet close in F major.

fields.value: The Griller String Quartet (string quartet), Sidney Griller (violin), Jack O’Brien (violin), Philip Burton (viola), Colin Hampton (cello)
fields.note: The two photographed disc labels explicitly name all four players and their instruments. They do not label the violin chairs first and second; the dossier does not expand their order into a chair attribution.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original quartet scoring; movement III. The Archive’s combined III–IV designation is disputed.
fields.note: The exact selected 1092.62-second MP3 is retained without truncation or substitution. Its analysed structure supports the five alternating spans of III, at approximately 0, 214, 340, 558 and 686 seconds, followed by slow music through the endpoint. The required report does not establish an A major march or the IV–V link. Supplementary upper-band inspection finds an F-centred ending; verifier VerH independently checked the selected file’s final37.6s against the score and also found the F ending of III, not IV’s dominant recitative. These are score/audio-feature correspondences, not an aural or complete bar-aligned certification. No IV boundary or IV listening prose is invented. Performing edition, cuts, repeat observance and the completeness of the final played release remain unestablished.
alts: III–IV combined, as asserted by the Archive filename and catalogue metadata
III only, supported by the selected file’s five-span design and independently checked F-centred endpoint

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition and the nineteenth-century Breitkopf & Härtel quartet score are public domain.
fields.note: The quartet was composed in 1825; Beethoven died in 1827. The consulted Beethovens Werke engraving, plate B.51, is catalogued as the 1863 edition and Public Domain. This does not clear an unidentified later performing edition or the sleeve author’s prose.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis only: the recording was published before 1963; US status is not established.
fields.note: The admitted basis is eu-published-before-1963, using the Archive’s 1952 catalogue date for this identified London LLP318 issue. The printed sleeve carries a 1951 copyright notice, corroborating an early-1950s package but not independently establishing the first publication year of the sound recording. A recording published by 1952 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term before 1 November 2013; the 2011 extension applies to recordings still protected on that date. This is territorial, not a Creative Commons grant or worldwide clearance. The US 1947–1956 term is longer, and no US public-domain claim is made. The Archive item supplies no separate recording licence; availability online and Beethoven’s public-domain composition are not the admission basis.

composer.epithet: Composer known for a symphony built from a four-note motif and for the string quartets of his last years.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, where he learned operas as a member of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was expected to return. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him ceased to exist.
